title: Hand back the very same node

tests.expr: let t = Hashtbl.create 16 in let next = ref 0 in let a = make t next "x" in let b = make t next "x" in string_of_bool (a == b)
let t = Hashtbl.create 16 in let next = ref 0 in let a = make t next "x" in let b = make t next "y" in Printf.sprintf "%d %d" a.id b.id
let t = Hashtbl.create 16 in let next = ref 0 in let _ = make t next "x" in let _ = make t next "y" in let _ = make t next "x" in string_of_int (make t next "z").id
let t = Hashtbl.create 16 in let next = ref 0 in let a = make t next "x" in let b = make t next "y" in string_of_bool (a == b)
let t = Hashtbl.create 16 in let next = ref 0 in let _ = make t next "x" in let _ = make t next "y" in string_of_int (make t next "x").id
let t1 = Hashtbl.create 16 in let n1 = ref 0 in let t2 = Hashtbl.create 16 in let n2 = ref 0 in let _ = make t1 n1 "a" in string_of_int (make t2 n2 "b").id
let t = Hashtbl.create 16 in let next = ref 0 in for _ = 1 to 100 do ignore (make t next "s") done; Printf.sprintf "%d %d" (Hashtbl.length t) !next
let t = Hashtbl.create 16 in let next = ref 0 in let a = make t next "x" in string_of_bool (a.op = "x" && a.src = [])

hints: Two lines are wrong. One is on the `Some n` line, the other is something missing after the new node is built.
`{ n with op = op }` builds a copy, and a copy is not `==` to the original. Return `n` itself.
After building the new node, move the counter on with `incr next`, so the next new node gets the next number.
explain: On a hit the reference returns the stored `n` itself, so every caller that asks for the same op holds the very same node and `==` is true. On a miss it builds the node with `id = !next`, runs `incr next` so no two nodes share a number, saves the node in the table and returns it.
